newsitem.title: CYPRUS: How Iraq's neighbours view crisis with U.S..
newsitem.headline: How Iraq's neighbours view crisis with U.S..

text.p: Iraq's military support for a Kurdish faction in northern Iraq and the U.S. missile strikes that followed against targets in the south posed tricky problems for Iraq's neighbours.
Following are viewpoints from countries bordering Iraq:
TURKEY - Iraq's military action in its breakaway north highlighted risks for Turkey's new Islamist-led government.
Necmettin Erbakan, NATO member Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, has touted accommodation with Iraq, Iran and Syria to supplement or even replace Ankara's pro-Western approach.
Turkey also counted on fat pipeline fees for carrying Iraqi oil to Western markets and eventual restoration of trade with Baghdad, once its third biggest partner. Now both are at risk.

A $2 billion oil-for-food deal that would have returned Iraq to world oil markets for the first time in six years has been put off. "What has happened in the region has changed the balance of power unexpectedly. Erbakan's plan for a four-way pact is now a dream," analyst Sami Kohen told Reuters.

IRAN - Washington recently tightened the sanctions screw on Iran, one country on a list of "rogue regimes" it says sponsor terrorism, so Iran's government and people are relieved that U.S. attention has switched to Iraq, their western neighbour and enemy in the 1980-88 war.

Iran accuses U.S. President Bill Clinton of playing politics by adopting a tough-guy image ahead of November's election. It also accuses the Americans of looking for reasons to justify a permanent U.S. presence in the Gulf.
President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani has denied U.S. and Iraqi charges of meddling in northern Iraq, saying Iran only targeted its own "anti-revolutionary elements" (rebel Kurds) based there.
KUWAIT - The government and many Kuwaitis welcomed an expanded air exclusion zone in southern Iraq and said Kuwait was now safer than at any time since Iraq's 1990-91 occupation.
"Kuwait is safe from Iraqi evil and from any recklessness that the Iraqi regime might perpetrate," said Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah.
But some ordinary Kuwaitis had doubts, saying heightened tension damaged business confidence in the small, oil exporting country and would complicate its ties to some other Arab states.
"In the Arab world, Kuwaitis will be seen to be at fault for these attacks through their association with America," said businessman Waleed al-Huwail.
SAUDI ARABIA - The dominant Gulf Arab power has maintained official silence on the U.S. attacks. Diplomats said Riyadh was eager to make clear to its citizens that it was not taking part.
But Washington's main Arab ally shows no sympathy for Iraq's President Saddam Hussein, with whom it refuses all contact, often seeking to block talks between Iraq and regional allies.
It took King Fahd six years to make up with Jordan's King Hussein, seen as an Iraq sympathiser in the Gulf crisis. "It will take him forever to talk again to Saddam," said one analyst.
The Gulf War allies continue to fly missions from Saudi Arabia to police the no-fly zone in southern Iraq -- in Riyadh's view a legitimate measure to contain Baghdad.

Analysts say Riyadh finds it difficult to explain to its people that the attacks were justified at a time when it is trying to tackle the issue of the need for a U.S. military presence in the conservative kingdom. Twenty-four Americans and two Indians were killed in two separate bomb attacks in Saudi Arabia in November and June against U.S. military interests.
JORDAN - Jordan, which has called for change in Baghdad since two powerful sons-in-law of Saddam defected to Amman in August 1995, steered clear of condemning the U.S. strikes.
But it expressed concern about possible Iranian involvement in northern Iraq, which it fears could lead to the fragmentation of Jordan's powerful neighbour.
"We are treading a very difficult line," said one official source. "But there has been an attack on an Arab country, which we do not like, and we also have economic links with Iraq."
Many Jordanians are sympathetic to Baghdad, which remains a key market for their goods and supplier of their oil needs at concessionary rates, partly in repayment of an old debt.

SYRIA - Despite cool relations with Saddam's government dating back more than 16 years, Syria responded to the U.S. attacks with outrage on both official and popular levels. A Foreign Ministry spokesman called the strikes a violation of the U.N. charter and international law.

Officials say it was different when Syria joined a U.S.-led force that drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait. "Now the United States is violating the sovereignty of an Arab country as Iraq violated the sovereignty of Kuwait when it occupied it in August 1990," one said. Syria sided with Iran in the Iran-Iraq war.
